title: SpaceX Launches Classified USSF-153 Mission from Vandenberg
detail: SpaceX launched the classified USSF-153 mission for the U.S. Space Force at 11:42 a.m. EDT (8:42 a.m. PDT / 15:42 UTC) on September 10, 2026, from Space Launch Complex 4E at Vandenberg Space Force Base. The Falcon 9 first-stage booster, flying its 27th mission after previously supporting Crew-7, CRS-29, PACE, Transporter-10, EarthCARE, NROL-186, Transporter-13, TRACERS, NROL-48, COSMO-SkyMed Second Generation FM3, and 16 Starlink missions, landed on the droneship 'Of Course I Still Love You' in the Pacific roughly 8.5 minutes after liftoff — the 660th Falcon booster landing in SpaceX history (224th on that vessel). USSF-153 was SpaceX's 104th Falcon 9 launch of 2026. As with most national security missions, Space Systems Command disclosed no payload details ('specific details about the mission and payload are protected'), though the rocket's stage drop zones matched prior Starlink Group 15 launches, suggesting the payload may be built on SpaceX's hardened Starshield satellite bus.

media.caption: Falcon 9 lifts off from Vandenberg Space Force Base carrying the classified USSF-153 mission, September 10, 2026

title: UK Discloses Nearly $40 Million in Spending on SpaceX Starlink and Starshield
detail: Britain's Ministry of Defence disclosed, in response to a Reuters freedom-of-information request, that it has spent nearly $40 million on SpaceX satellite services — about £13 million ($17.6 million) on Starshield, SpaceX's hardened military/intelligence variant of Starlink, and £16.5 million on standard Starlink — making the UK the first country outside the US to publicly confirm adopting Starshield. The MoD operates roughly 1,000 Starshield terminals and 500 Starlink terminals; it began using Starlink in mid-2022, moved operational military traffic to Starshield airtime in 2024 after SpaceX restricted plain Starlink to morale, welfare, recreation and training use, and bought its first dedicated Starshield terminals in 2025. Starshield pricing in Britain runs £5,500/month for 5TB of data or £25,000/month unlimited (plus £4,000-£7,000 per terminal), versus £1,830/month for 2TB on business Starlink. New Zealand is separately testing Starshield, and the US government alone has awarded SpaceX over $6 billion in multi-year Starshield contracts.

media.caption: Britain's Ministry of Defence has spent nearly $40 million on SpaceX Starlink and Starshield satellite services

title: SpaceX Slows AI Data Center Buildout After Outages, Reshuffles Leadership
detail: SpaceX is overhauling its rapid AI data-center expansion after an outage left multiple Colossus facilities in Tennessee and Mississippi without backup power and cooling, disrupting Grok model training, per The Information. The company is now installing backup power and cooling systems and running more thorough testing before facilities go live, reversing its previous build-fast-fix-later approach; a mismatch between older Hopper-generation and newer Blackwell GPUs at Colossus 1, plus latency between facilities more than 10 miles apart, had also slowed cluster performance. Elon Musk reassigned Starlink executive Michael Nicolls to lead AI infrastructure after several data-center executives departed, backfilling with staff pulled from the rocket and Starlink programs. The slowdown comes as SpaceX races a September 30 deadline under its deal to supply Google with roughly 110,000 Nvidia GPUs for $920 million/month — after a grace period, Google can terminate, cut the GPU allocation, or reduce payments if SpaceX misses it. SpaceX is also building an in-house turbine foundry in Bastrop, Texas to speed power deployment. SPCX traded up slightly (~$149.87, +1.14%) on the news; Goldman Sachs projects SpaceX's AI revenue could reach $322 billion by 2030, up from $3.2 billion in 2025.

media.caption: SpaceX reworks its AI data-center buildout after outages disrupted Grok training
